title: Match-mount two tyres: red dot to a wheel's low-point mark, else yellow to the valve
instruction: Mount a tyre on each wheel on the changer turntables, turning each tyre so its marks line up with the wheel the way tyre makers require, then let go. The red and yellow dots are on the tyre sidewalls. The small post on each wheel is the valve stem, and the white dot on one wheel is its low-point mark.
context: Tyre fitters in car dealers, fleet garages and tyre shops match-mount tyres every day. Many tyres carry two sidewall dots: red, the point of maximum radial force variation, and yellow, the lightest point. Yokohama's match-mounting instructions say the red dot is lined up with the wheel's point of minimum radial runout, marked on many wheels by a coloured dot or a notch (steel wheels often carry a white dot), and that when the wheel has no such mark the weight method is used instead: the yellow dot goes to the valve stem, the wheel's heavy point. A tyre mounted the wrong way round needs more balance weight or causes a vibration, and the shop has to break the bead and turn it. Knowing only 'yellow to the valve' gets one of these wheels right; the precedence rule gets both. Here two wheels stand on changer turntables, one marked and one not, and a tyre lies in front of each.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Angles about an axis are seen from above, counter-clockwise from +x (0 points straight away from the arms, 90 to the left). A tyre fitter's bench at about 1:10; everything except the two tyres is fixed to the table. (1) Two changer turntables: dark grey painted steel discs, 54 mm across, 6 mm thick, centred at x 34.0 cm, y +15.0 cm (A, left) and y -15.0 cm (B, right). (2) Two wheels: silver painted steel cylinders, 36 mm across, 24 mm tall, each standing on its turntable on the same axis (top face 30 mm above the table). (3) Two valve stems: black rubber posts, 6 mm across, 8 mm tall, standing on each wheel's top face, centred 10 mm from its axis at 0 degrees. (4) Low-point mark: a white painted dot, 8 mm across, 1 mm thick, on wheel A's top face only, centred 10 mm from its axis at 120 degrees. Wheel B has no mark. (5) Two tyres, loose and identical: black solid rubber rings, 64 mm across the outside, a 46 mm bore, 22 mm tall, 40 g each; the tread and the bore are 36 overlapping round ribs 9 mm across, so both are scalloped about 0.7 mm deep. On each tyre's top sidewall, 27.5 mm from its centre, are two painted dots, 7 mm across and 0.6 mm thick: a red one and a yellow one 100 degrees counter-clockwise of it. Tyre A lies flat, dots up, centred at x 24.0 cm, y +15.0 cm, its red dot toward 60 degrees (yellow toward 160). Tyre B lies flat, dots up, centred at x 24.0 cm, y -15.0 cm, its red dot toward -40 degrees (yellow toward 60). The tyre's bore clears a wheel by 5 mm all round, and the valve stem and the mark lie inside the bore, so a tyre lowered over a wheel rests on the turntable with both still in view. Seated, a tyre's top is 2 mm below the wheel's top face. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: End state, read at the last step from the tyres' poses and both grippers (in a real trial: a ruler, a protractor and a top photo). 'Seated' on a wheel: the tyre's centre within 6 mm of the wheel's axis seen from above, its underside within 3 mm of the turntable's top, its axis within 5 degrees of vertical with the dots up, let go (each gripper's fingers at least 10 mm from the tyre: a gripper's fingers are taken as everything within reach of a pad's outer corner, half the finger gap plus 8 mm out and 13.5 mm across, around the 38 mm stretch back from the point between its pad tips) and still (over the last 1 s its centre moved at most 1.5 mm in each 0.5 s and its turn changed at most 2 degrees). A dot's angle is the direction from the tyre's centre to the dot's centre, seen from above. Wheel A (white mark) is correct when exactly one tyre is seated on it and that tyre's red dot is within 10 degrees of 120 degrees (the mark). Wheel B (no mark) is correct when exactly one tyre is seated on it and that tyre's yellow dot is within 10 degrees of 0 degrees (the valve stem). Either tyre may go on either wheel. Score: 1.0 both wheels correct (success, held 1 s); 0.5 exactly one wheel correct; 0.25 at least one tyre seated but no wheel correct; 0 no tyre seated (tyres left on the table, stacked on a wheel's top, held, still moving, tilted, upside down or anywhere else). Examples: yellow dot to the valve on both wheels 0.5 (wheel B only); red dot to the valve on both 0.25; both tyres mounted at their starting turn 0.25; both right but one still held 0.5. The 10 degree window is 4.8 mm of arc at the dots; a tyre at a random turn falls inside it 5.6% of the time.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with the simulator's default friction, at about 1:10. Each tyre is one rigid rubber ring (36 overlapping ribs, so its tread and bore are scalloped 0.7 mm) that drops over a plain fixed wheel onto the turntable: no beads, inflation, lubricant or balancing. The valve stem and the low-point mark are on the wheel's top face inside the tyre's bore, so both stay in view. What the rule sets, the tyre's turn about the wheel's axis, is modelled exactly.
reset_notes: Lay the two tyres back flat, dots up: tyre A centred at x 24.0 cm, y +15.0 cm with its red dot toward 60 degrees (yellow at 160), tyre B centred at x 24.0 cm, y -15.0 cm with its red dot toward -40 degrees (yellow at 60). Angles are seen from above, counter-clockwise from +x (straight away from the arms). Nothing is consumed; the turntables, wheels, valve stems and mark are fixed.
